papers.title: Cancer-related cognitive impairment in adult cancer survivors: a clinical practice review for healthcare providers.
papers.abstract: PURPOSE: Cancer-related cognitive impairment (CRCI) is a decline in cognitive function associated with cancer and its treatments, affecting approximately 60-75% of individuals with cancer. This review provides an evidence-based overview of the causes, assessment, and management of CRCI across the cancer continuum. METHODS: A narrative literature review was conducted using peer-reviewed studies, clinical practice guidelines, systematic reviews, and expert consensus recommendations examining CRCI in adult cancer populations. The review focused on the biological and psychosocial contributors to CRCI, methods of assessment and diagnosis, and current evidence supporting pharmacological and non-pharmacological interventions. RESULTS: CRCI is a multifactorial condition associated with chemotherapy, endocrine therapy, radiotherapy, surgery, psychological distress, and lifestyle factors. Proposed mechanisms include neuroinflammation, oxidative stress, neurotoxicity, hormonal dysregulation, and psychosocial influences such as anxiety, depression, and fatigue. Assessment should incorporate both patient-reported cognitive concerns and objective neuropsychological testing, while also evaluating potentially reversible contributors including sleep disturbances, pain, medication effects, and emotional distress. Current evidence supports non-pharmacological interventions as first-line management, with physical activity and cognitive rehabilitation demonstrating the strongest benefits. Additional strategies including mindfulness-based interventions, psychoeducation, compensatory techniques, and healthy lifestyle modifications may further improve cognitive outcomes. Pharmacological therapies, including psychostimulants and neuroprotective agents, have shown inconsistent results and are not routinely recommended. CONCLUSION: CRCI is a prevalent and clinically significant survivorship issue that requires greater recognition within oncology care. Routine screening, comprehensive assessment, and individualized management strategies can help mitigate cognitive symptoms and improve functional outcomes. Further research is needed to develop standardized screening tools, establish evidence-based treatment pathways, and improve integration of CRCI care into routine oncology practice.

papers.title: Evaluating smartphone-based interventions for anxiety and depressive symptoms: A randomized controlled trial.
papers.abstract: OBJECTIVE: The study evaluated the impact of two smartphone-based interventions on anxiety and depression symptoms during the COVID-19 pandemic. METHOD: Racially and ethnically diverse adults from the United States (US) with elevated anxiety and/or depression (N = 822; 64.4% female; M RESULTS: There was a high degree of engagement for both groups. For our primary analysis, between-group differences at the 6-month primary endpoint were small and not statistically significant for anxiety and depression. Within-person effect sizes indicated decreases in anxiety, depression, probable clinical anxiety and/or depression disorder status, anxiety sensitivity, and COVID-19 fear through the follow-up. Exploratory subgroup analyses suggested variable patterns of within-condition change across racial and ethnic groups, but these analyses were not powered to test moderation or equivalence. CONCLUSIONS: Findings indicated that two low cost and highly disseminatable digital interventions that targeted distinct psychological processes offered clinical benefit among a diverse sample of adults in the US during the COVID-19 pandemic.

papers.title: Mental health distress among undergraduate nursing students in Egypt: associations with self-concealment, alexithymia, and personality traits in a cross-sectional study.
papers.abstract: BACKGROUND: Psychological distress among nursing students is a major concern in nursing education. Difficulties in emotional processing and stable personality traits may be associated with depression, anxiety, and stress, yet self-concealment, alexithymia, and personality traits have rarely been examined together in undergraduate nursing students, particularly in Egypt. This study aimed to examine how self-concealment, alexithymia, and personality traits are associated with depression, anxiety, and stress among undergraduate nursing students. METHODS: A cross-sectional correlational study was conducted among 353 undergraduate nursing students at the Faculty of Nursing, Alexandria University, Egypt. Participants were recruited using proportionate stratified random sampling across the four academic years. Data were collected using a socio-demographic and academic questionnaire, the Self-Concealment Scale, the Toronto Alexithymia Scale-20, the NEO Five-Factor Inventory, and the Depression Anxiety Stress Scales-21. Data were analyzed using descriptive statistics, Pearson correlation coefficients, independent-samples t-tests, one-way analyses of variance, and multiple linear regression. RESULTS: Psychological distress symptoms were common on self-reported screening measures, and anxiety showed the greatest severity, with 53.8% of participants falling in the extremely severe symptom range. These classifications reflect screening scores rather than clinical diagnoses. Self-concealment and alexithymia were positively associated with depression, anxiety, and stress. The adjusted regression models explained 53.1% of the variance in depression, 48.9% in anxiety, and 47.5% in stress. Self-concealment and alexithymia remained significant correlates across all three adjusted models; self-concealment showed the largest standardized coefficient for anxiety and stress, whereas alexithymia showed the largest standardized coefficient for depression. CONCLUSIONS: Psychological distress symptoms in nursing students were associated with self-concealment, alexithymia, and selected personality traits. The findings support early confidential screening, timely access to counseling through clear referral pathways, and targeted resilience-, mindfulness-, peer-support-, and emotion-focused programs within nursing education. Because the design was cross-sectional, these associations should not be interpreted causally.
